claim: C. elegans nrx-1/neurexin directs divergent connectivity through differential actions at synapses with partnering neurons and muscles.
source: We report that C. elegans nrx-1/neurexin directs divergent connectivity through differential actions at synapses with partnering neurons and muscles.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental results including receptor clustering assays, calcium imaging, and behavioral analysis.

claim: Cholinergic outputs onto GABAergic neurons are located at previously undefined spine-like protrusions from GABAergic dendrites.
source: We show that cholinergic outputs onto neurons are, unexpectedly, located at previously undefined spine-like protrusions from GABAergic dendrites.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing ACR-12 receptor clusters at dendritic protrusions (Figure 1).

claim: Spine-like features and cholinergic receptor clustering are disrupted in the absence of nrx-1.
source: Both these spine-like features and cholinergic receptor clustering are strikingly disrupted in the absence of nrx-1.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of spine-like protrusions and ACR-12 receptor clusters in nrx-1 mutants compared to wild type (Figures 3, 4).

claim: Excitatory transmission onto GABAergic neurons, but not neuromuscular transmission, is disrupted in nrx-1 mutants.
source: Excitatory transmission onto GABAergic neurons, but not neuromuscular transmission, is also disrupted.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing reduced GABA neuron responses but normal muscle responses in nrx-1 mutants (Figure 7).

claim: NRX-1 located at presynaptic sites specifically directs postsynaptic development in GABAergic neurons.
source: Our data indicate that NRX-1 located at presynaptic sites specifically directs postsynaptic development in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell-specific rescue experiments showing that cholinergic expression of nrx-1 rescues postsynaptic defects in GABAergic neurons (Figure 5).

claim: Individual neurons can direct differential patterns of connectivity with their post-synaptic partners through partner-specific utilization of synaptic organizers.
source: Our findings provide evidence that individual neurons can direct differential patterns of connectivity with their post-synaptic partners through partner-specific utilization of synaptic organizers, offering a novel view into molecular control of divergent connectivity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the differential requirement of nrx-1 for GABAergic versus muscle synapses.

claim: ACR-12 receptors in GABAergic motor neurons are clustered opposite cholinergic terminals.
source: Prior work showed that ACR-12 receptors in GABAergic motor neurons are clustered opposite cholinergic terminals and GABAergic expression of ACR-12::GFP rescues acr-12 mutant phenotypes (Barbagallo et al., 2017; Petrash et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Postsynaptic ACR-12::GFP clusters relocate appropriately during developmental synaptic remodeling of DD neurons.
source: Moreover, postsynaptic ACR-12::GFP clusters relocate appropriately during developmental synaptic remodeling of the DD neurons, suggesting these clusters faithfully report synaptic inputs (He et al., 2015; Howell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: In adults, the anterior DD1 process extends from the soma to enter the ventral nerve cord fascicle (the dendritic compartment), where approximately 26 synaptic inputs from cholinergic neurons are concentrated.
source: In adults, the anterior DD1 process extends from the soma to enter the ventral nerve cord fascicle (the dendritic compartment), where prior EM studies show that approximately 26 synaptic inputs from cholinergic neurons are concentrated (the synaptic region, Figure 1C,D) (White et al., 1978, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior EM studies.

claim: The DD1 process crosses the longitudinal midline of the worm via a commissural connection and enters the dorsal nerve cord where it forms en passant synaptic outputs onto body wall muscles.
source: The process then crosses the longitudinal midline of the worm via a commissural connection and enters the dorsal nerve cord where it forms en passant synaptic outputs onto body wall muscles (the axonal compartment) (Figure 1A,B) (White et al., 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and Figure 1.

claim: ACR-12::GFP receptor clusters in DD1 are confined to the synaptic region of the ventral dendritic process in the mature animal.
source: We find that ACR-12::GFP receptor clusters in DD1 are confined to the synaptic region of the ventral dendritic process in the mature animal (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1C.

claim: The majority of ACR-12::GFP clusters do not appear localized to the shaft of the primary DD1 dendritic process, instead appearing to protrude from the primary DD1 dendrite shaft.
source: Surprisingly, we noted that the majority of ACR-12::GFP clusters do not appear localized to the shaft of the primary DD1 dendritic process, instead appearing to protrude from the primary DD1 dendrite shaft (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1C.

claim: Finger-like structures (~0.3–1 μm in length) project outward from the DD1 dendrite in the synaptic region.
source: Intriguingly, we noted finger-like structures (~0.3–1 μm in length) projecting outward from the DD1 dendrite in this region (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Spine-like structures are not present in the asynaptic region of the DD1 process immediately adjacent to the cell soma.
source: In contrast, these structures are not present in the asynaptic region of the process immediately adjacent to the cell soma (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1D.

claim: Spine-like protrusions are most clearly identifiable with specific labeling of DD neurons.
source: These protrusions are obscured by the processes of other ventral cord neurons when using promoters that provide for more broad expression (e.g. unc-47), and are therefore most clearly identifiable with specific labeling of DD neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by comparison images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Spine-like protrusions are clearly identifiable in the dendrites of more posterior DD neurons.
source: Spine-like protrusions are also clearly identifiable in the dendrites of more posterior DD neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), but are not apparent in a related class of post-embryonic born, ventrally directed GABAergic (VD) neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), although the density of VD processes may complicate their detection.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: The dendritic protrusions concentrate clusters of ACR-12 receptors at their tips.
source: The dendritic protrusions concentrate clusters of ACR-12 receptors at their tips (Figure 1E), and over 60% of ACR-12::GFP clusters appear localized to protrusions (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Over 60% of ACR-12::GFP clusters appear localized to protrusions.
source: The dendritic protrusions concentrate clusters of ACR-12 receptors at their tips (Figure 1E), and over 60% of ACR-12::GFP clusters appear localized to protrusions (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 1F showing approximately 67% of clusters associated with protrusions.

claim: The dendritic protrusions increase in abundance through larval development.
source: The dendritic protrusions increase in abundance through larval development, and this increase correlates well with a similar developmental increase in ACR-12::GFP receptor clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by developmental time course data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase in dendritic protrusions correlates well with a similar developmental increase in ACR-12::GFP receptor clusters.
source: The dendritic protrusions increase in abundance through larval development, and this increase correlates well with a similar developmental increase in ACR-12::GFP receptor clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by developmental time course data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dendritic protrusions and ACR-12 receptor clusters are both located opposite clusters of cholinergic synaptic vesicles.
source: We found that dendritic protrusions and ACR-12 receptor clusters are both located opposite clusters of cholinergic synaptic vesicles (Figure 2A,B), indicating that these likely represent mature synapses.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing colocalization in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: ACR-12 receptors with an extracellular HA tag are accessible to antibody labeling in live animals, confirming cell surface localization.
source: Injection of Alexa594 conjugated anti-HA antibody into live transgenic animals expressing this construct produces specific labeling in the DD1 synaptic region, and is also evident in coelomocytes (scavenger cells that take up excess antibody), confirming successful injection (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by antibody injection experiments and imaging in Figure 2C.

claim: The anti-HA signal colocalizes with ACR-12::GFP clusters in the synaptic region of DD1, but is not evident in the cell soma.
source: The anti-HA signal colocalizes with ACR-12::GFP clusters in the synaptic region of DD1, but is not evident in the cell soma.
evidence: Supported by antibody injection experiments and imaging in Figure 2C.

claim: The intracellular GFP moiety produces fluorescence that is evident in both the soma and the synaptic region of the dendrite, representing both synaptic and internal receptor pools.
source: In contrast, the intracellular GFP moiety produces fluorescence that is evident in both the soma and the synaptic region of the dendrite, representing both synaptic and internal receptor pools (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 2C showing GFP fluorescence in both locations.

claim: Injection of anti-GFP antibody did not produce specific labeling, confirming that the intracellularly positioned GFP is not accessible to antibody.
source: Injection of anti-GFP antibody did not produce specific labeling, confirming that the intracellularly positioned GFP is not accessible to antibody (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by control antibody injection experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ACR-12 is incorporated into mature receptor complexes that are specifically targeted for transport to DD neuron dendrites, and reside on the cell surface at post-synaptic sites.
source: Our analysis of ACR-12 localization in DD1 indicates that ACR-12 is incorporated into mature receptor complexes that are specifically targeted for transport to DD neuron dendrites, and reside on the cell surface at post-synaptic sites.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the antibody labeling experiments and imaging data.

claim: Single mutations in the acetylcholine receptor subunit genes unc-38, unc-63, lev-1 or unc-29 strongly decrease ACR-12::GFP clustering.
source: We found that single mutations in the acetylcholine receptor subunit genes unc-38, unc-63, lev-1 or unc-29 strongly decrease ACR-12::GFP clustering.
evidence: Supported by quantification of ACR-12::GFP clusters in various mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: In wild type, approximately 15 receptor clusters are observed within the DD1 synaptic region.
source: In wild type, we observe approximately 15 receptor clusters within the DD1 synaptic region.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the imaging data.

claim: ACR-12::GFP clusters are eliminated almost completely with mutation of unc-38, unc-63, lev-1, or unc-29 subunit genes.
source: These clusters are eliminated almost completely with mutation of these subunit genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Mutations in other nAChR subunit genes with previously reported neuronal expression, such as acr-9 and acr-14, do not disrupt synaptic ACR-12 clustering.
source: In contrast, mutations in other nAChR subunit genes with previously reported neuronal expression, such as acr-9 and acr-14 (Cinar et al., 2005; Fox et al., 2005), do not disrupt synaptic ACR-12 clustering (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in genes important for AChR assembly and trafficking (unc-50, unc-74, and ric-3) abolish synaptic clusters of ACR-12::GFP.
source: Mutations in genes important for AChR assembly and trafficking (unc-50, unc-74, and ric-3) (Boulin et al., 2008; Eimer et al., 2007; Halevi et al., 2002; Haugstetter et al., 2005) also abolish synaptic clusters of ACR-12::GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C and citations to prior work.

claim: GABA neuron-specific expression of wild type cDNAs encoding individual AChR subunits or accessory proteins in the respective mutants is sufficient to restore ACR-12 clustering to wild type levels.
source: GABA neuron-specific expression of wild type cDNAs encoding individual AChR subunits (UNC-63 or UNC-38) or accessory proteins in the respective mutants is sufficient to restore ACR-12 clustering to wild type levels, providing support that both gene classes act cell-autonomously in GABA neurons to promote receptor assembly, maturation and synaptic delivery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: AChR subunits and accessory proteins act cell-autonomously in GABA neurons to promote receptor assembly, maturation and synaptic delivery.
source: GABA neuron-specific expression of wild type cDNAs encoding individual AChR subunits (UNC-63 or UNC-38) or accessory proteins in the respective mutants is sufficient to restore ACR-12 clustering to wild type levels, providing support that both gene classes act cell-autonomously in GABA neurons to promote receptor assembly, maturation and synaptic delivery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Cell-specific expression of either UNC-29::GFP or UNC-63::GFP in DD neurons produces punctate labeling in the DD1 synaptic region that closely resembles ACR-12::GFP clustering.
source: Cell-specific expression of either UNC-29::GFP or UNC-63::GFP in DD neurons produces punctate labeling in the DD1 synaptic region that closely resembles ACR-12::GFP clustering (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutation of acr-12 significantly reduces UNC-29::GFP or UNC-63::GFP receptor clusters and fluorescence signal in the DD1 synaptic region.
source: Mutation of acr-12 in these transgenic animals significantly reduces UNC-29::GFP or UNC-63::GFP receptor clusters and fluorescence signal in the DD1 synaptic region (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E), providing further evidence that they coassemble with ACR-12.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: UNC-38, UNC-63, LEV-1, UNC-29 and ACR-12 subunits coassemble into a pentameric acetylcholine receptor in GABAergic neurons.
source: Together, our results indicate UNC-38, UNC-63, LEV-1, UNC-29 and ACR-12 subunits coassemble into a pentameric acetylcholine receptor in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic and imaging data showing interdependence of these subunits for receptor clustering.

claim: Mutation of the nrx-1 gene produces a ~70% reduction in ACR-12 receptor clustering.
source: Mutation of the nrx-1 gene (orange, Figure 3A) does not significantly affect transgene expression in GABAergic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D), but produces a ~70% reduction in ACR-12 receptor clustering (nrx-1(ok1649), p<0.0001) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 3A,B.

claim: nrx-1 encodes the sole C. elegans ortholog of the synaptic organizer neurexin.
source: nrx-1 encodes the sole C. elegans ortholog of the synaptic organizer neurexin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the C. elegans genome.

claim: Neurexin has been well documented to play roles in mammalian synapse formation and function.
source: Neurexin has been well documented to play roles in mammalian synapse formation and function (Chen et al., 2017; Dean et al., 2003; Graf et al., 2004; Missler et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: There are no appreciable alterations in the clustering of muscle AChRs in nrx-1 mutants.
source: Importantly, we do not observe appreciable alterations in the clustering of muscle AChRs in nrx-1 mutants (Figure 3C), similar to previously reported findings (Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by quantification of muscle AChR clusters in Figure 3C and citation to prior work.

claim: Presynaptic remodeling, as measured using the synaptic vesicle marker mCherry::RAB-3, proceeds normally in nrx-1 mutants.
source: Presynaptic remodeling, as measured using the synaptic vesicle marker mCherry::RAB-3, proceeds normally in nrx-1 mutants, indicating that this process does not require neurexin expression.
evidence: Supported by imaging of presynaptic markers during DD neuron remodeling in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The clustering of ACR-12 receptors is impaired both prior to and following remodeling in nrx-1 mutants.
source: The clustering of ACR-12 receptors, however, is impaired both prior to and following remodeling in nrx-1 mutants, suggesting that NRX-1 is required for receptor clustering in each of these developmental stages.
evidence: Supported by imaging of ACR-12 receptors during DD neuron remodeling in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The C. elegans nrx-1 locus encodes both long (nrx-1L) and short (nrx-1S) neurexin isoforms.
source: As is the case for mammals, the C. elegans nrx-1 locus encodes both long (nrx-1L) and short (nrx-1S) neurexin isoforms (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the nrx-1 gene structure, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The ok1649 allele generates an in-frame deletion, eliminating 861 bp predicted to encode an extracellular LNS domain.
source: The ok1649 allele generates an in-frame deletion, eliminating 861 bp predicted to encode an extracellular LNS domain, raising the possibility that partial NRX-1 function may still be present in this strain.
evidence: This is a description of the molecular nature of the ok1649 allele.

claim: All of the nrx-1 deletions tested disrupt ACR-12 receptor clustering in DD GABAergic neurons, with the most severe disruptions occurring in nrx-1(wy778) and nrx-1(nu485) mutants.
source: All of the deletions tested disrupt ACR-12 receptor clustering in DD GABAergic neurons, with the most severe disruptions occurring in nrx-1(wy778) and nrx-1(nu485) mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of ACR-12 receptor clusters in multiple nrx-1 alleles shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Significant disruption of ACR-12 receptor clustering occurs in the VD GABAergic neurons of nrx-1 mutants.
source: Strikingly, we also observe significant disruption of ACR-12 receptor clustering in the VD GABAergic neurons (Figure 3F,G) of nrx-1 mutants, indicating a requirement for nrx-1 at synapses onto both GABAergic neuron classes.
evidence: Supported by quantification of ACR-12 receptor clusters in VD neurons shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: The residual ACR-12 receptor clusters in nrx-1 mutants are present at the cell surface.
source: Antibody fluorescent signal clearly colocalizes with ACR-12::GFP fluorescence, providing evidence that the few remaining receptor clusters in nrx-1 mutants are present at the cell surface (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by antibody injection experiments in nrx-1 mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Neurexin is not essential for membrane insertion of ACR-12 receptors, although this process may occur less efficiently in nrx-1 mutants.
source: We interpret this result to indicate that neurexin is not essential for membrane insertion, although we can't rule out that this process may occur less efficiently in nrx-1 mutants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the antibody labeling data showing some surface receptors remain in nrx-1 mutants.

claim: Neurexin deletion (wy778) reduces UNC-29::GFP and UNC-63::GFP clusters in DD1 by 60%.
source: Neurexin deletion (wy778) reduces UNC-29::GFP and UNC-63::GFP clusters in DD1 by 60%, consistent with a requirement for neurexin in the proper localization of mature, heteromeric receptor complexes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: nrx-1 deletion does not appreciably disrupt the clustering of AMPA-type glutamate receptors in interneurons.
source: In contrast to our findings for GABAergic neurons, nrx-1 deletion does not appreciably disrupt the clustering of AMPA-type glutamate receptors in interneurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), consistent with the idea that neurexin is not globally required for the establishment of synaptic connectivity in worms.
evidence: Supported by imaging of GLR-1::GFP in nrx-1 mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: There is no appreciable decrease in cholinergic synaptic vesicle clusters in nrx-1 mutants.
source: Additionally, we do not observe an appreciable decrease in cholinergic synaptic vesicle clusters (acr-2::SNB-1::GFP), although this analysis does not rule out all potential presynaptic defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of SNB-1::GFP clusters in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Mutation of nlg-1 produces no appreciable defects in ACR-12 receptor clustering.
source: We find that mutation of nlg-1 produces no appreciable defects in ACR-12 receptor clustering (Figure 3A,B), indicating, surprisingly, that NRX-1 operates independently of NLG-1 to direct post-synaptic development in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by quantification of ACR-12 receptor clusters in nlg-1 mutants shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: NRX-1 operates independently of NLG-1 to direct post-synaptic development in GABAergic neurons.
source: We find that mutation of nlg-1 produces no appreciable defects in ACR-12 receptor clustering (Figure 3A,B), indicating, surprisingly, that NRX-1 operates independently of NLG-1 to direct post-synaptic development in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of effect of nlg-1 mutation on ACR-12 clustering.

claim: Wild type animals (at the L4 stage) have an average of 7–8 spiny protrusions within the synaptic region of the anterior DD1 dendrite.
source: Wild type animals (at the L4 stage) have an average of 7–8 of these spiny protrusions within the synaptic region of the anterior DD1 dendrite (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: nrx-1 mutants have strikingly reduced numbers of spiny protrusions.
source: In contrast, nrx-1 mutants have strikingly reduced numbers of spiny protrusions. For example, only two spiny protrusions are visible on average in DD1 dendrites of nrx-1(ok1649), and nrx-1(wy778) mutants show a near complete absence of spines (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Only two spiny protrusions are visible on average in DD1 dendrites of nrx-1(ok1649).
source: For example, only two spiny protrusions are visible on average in DD1 dendrites of nrx-1(ok1649), and nrx-1(wy778) mutants show a near complete absence of spines (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: nrx-1(wy778) mutants show a near complete absence of spines.
source: For example, only two spiny protrusions are visible on average in DD1 dendrites of nrx-1(ok1649), and nrx-1(wy778) mutants show a near complete absence of spines (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: nrx-1 deletion disrupts both ACR-12 receptor clustering and spine outgrowth in posterior DD neurons to a similar extent as observed for DD1.
source: nrx-1 deletion disrupts both ACR-12 receptor clustering and spine outgrowth in posterior DD neurons to a similar extent as observed for DD1 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the requirement for nrx-1 is shared across DD neurons.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Roughly 15% of the receptor clusters remaining in nrx-1(ok1649) mutants are associated with the remaining spines (compared with 67% in wild type).
source: Roughly 15% of the receptor clusters remaining in nrx-1(ok1649) mutants are associated with the remaining spines (compared with 67% in wild type).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the imaging data.

claim: The number of dendritic receptor clusters is not appreciably altered by nrx-1 deletion.
source: In contrast, the number of dendritic receptor clusters is not appreciably altered by nrx-1 deletion (p=0.67, student's t test), suggesting NRX-1 may preferentially regulate spine-associated receptor clusters in DD neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the imaging data with statistical analysis.

claim: NRX-1 may preferentially regulate spine-associated receptor clusters in DD neurons.
source: In contrast, the number of dendritic receptor clusters is not appreciably altered by nrx-1 deletion (p=0.67, student's t test), suggesting NRX-1 may preferentially regulate spine-associated receptor clusters in DD neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the differential effects on spine-associated versus dendritic clusters.

claim: nrx-1 deletion significantly reduces spiny protrusions in L2 animals (the earliest stage at which they are visible).
source: nrx-1 deletion also significantly reduces spiny protrusions in L2 animals (the earliest stage at which they are visible) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that neurexin is required for initial spine outgrowth, although an additional role in maintenance is also possible.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neurexin is required for initial spine outgrowth, although an additional role in maintenance is also possible.
source: nrx-1 deletion also significantly reduces spiny protrusions in L2 animals (the earliest stage at which they are visible) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that neurexin is required for initial spine outgrowth, although an additional role in maintenance is also possible.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the developmental timing data.

claim: Mutation of nlg-1 does not alter spine number.
source: In accordance with our finding that nlg-1 is not required for ACR-12::GFP localization, mutation of nlg-1 does not alter spine number (Figure 4A,B), arguing against an essential role for neuroligin in the formation of cholinergic synapses with GABAergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: Spine number is not appreciably altered in either acr-12 or unc-63 mutants.
source: Likewise, spine number is not appreciably altered in either acr-12 or unc-63 mutants (Figure 4A,B), indicating that spine outgrowth proceeds normally in the absence of functional ACR-12 receptors.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: Spine outgrowth proceeds normally in the absence of functional ACR-12 receptors.
source: Likewise, spine number is not appreciably altered in either acr-12 or unc-63 mutants (Figure 4A,B), indicating that spine outgrowth proceeds normally in the absence of functional ACR-12 receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of effect of acr-12 or unc-63 mutations on spine number.

claim: A nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter is strongly expressed in cholinergic motor neurons.
source: We first examined expression of a nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter incorporating ~4.8 kb of sequence upstream of the nrx-1L start site, and found that this reporter is strongly expressed in cholinergic motor neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by imaging of the nrx-1L::GFP reporter in Figure 5A.

claim: Cholinergic nrx-1L expression reverses the ACR-12 clustering defects of nrx-1(wy778) mutants.
source: We found that cholinergic nrx-1L expression reverses the ACR-12 clustering defects of nrx-1(wy778) mutants, while expression in either GABAergic neurons or muscles fails to rescue (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Expression of nrx-1L in either GABAergic neurons or muscles fails to rescue ACR-12 clustering defects in nrx-1 mutants.
source: We found that cholinergic nrx-1L expression reverses the ACR-12 clustering defects of nrx-1(wy778) mutants, while expression in either GABAergic neurons or muscles fails to rescue (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Supported by cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Cholinergic expression of nrx-1L restores spine-like protrusions in nrx-1 mutants.
source: Notably, cholinergic expression of nrx-1L also restores spine-like protrusions in nrx-1 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Presynaptic NRX-1 acts non-autonomously to direct post-synaptic assembly in GABAergic neurons.
source: Thus, our results suggest that presynaptic NRX-1 acts non-autonomously to direct post-synaptic assembly in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell-specific rescue experiments showing cholinergic expression rescues postsynaptic defects.

claim: Expression of unc-129::NRX-1L::GFP produces discrete puncta along the dorsal nerve cord where the synaptic outputs of DA/DB neurons are located.
source: Expression of unc-129::NRX-1L::GFP produces discrete puncta along the dorsal nerve cord where the synaptic outputs of DA/DB neurons are located (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 5E.

claim: NRX-1L::GFP clusters colocalize with clusters of mCherry::RAB-3 fluorescence, providing evidence that NRX-1L is preferentially localized to cholinergic presynaptic sites.
source: NRX-1L::GFP clusters colocalize with clusters of mCherry::RAB-3 fluorescence, providing evidence that NRX-1L is preferentially localized to cholinergic presynaptic sites (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by colocalization imaging in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Cholinergic expression of a rescuing transgene lacking the PDZ binding motif (nrx-1LΔPDZ) in nrx-1 mutants can rescue ACR-12 clustering defects.
source: Intriguingly, cholinergic expression of a rescuing transgene lacking the PDZ binding motif located at the intracellular NRX-1 C-terminus (nrx-1LΔPDZ) in nrx-1 mutants can also rescue ACR-12 clustering defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: NRX-1LΔPDZ::GFP is exclusively expressed in cholinergic axons and partially colocalizes with mCherry::RAB-3 fluorescence.
source: NRX-1LΔPDZ::GFP is exclusively expressed in cholinergic axons and partially colocalizes with mCherry::RAB-3 fluorescence, indicating that NRX-1 presynaptic localization and function is possible without PDZ protein binding via this motif (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: NRX-1 presynaptic localization and function is possible without PDZ protein binding via the C-terminal PDZ binding motif.
source: NRX-1LΔPDZ::GFP is exclusively expressed in cholinergic axons and partially colocalizes with mCherry::RAB-3 fluorescence, indicating that NRX-1 presynaptic localization and function is possible without PDZ protein binding via this motif (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue and localization data for the ΔPDZ construct.

claim: Loss of nlg-1 function does not affect the axonal localization of NRX-1L::GFP.
source: Loss of nlg-1 function does not affect the axonal localization of NRX-1L::GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,C–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,C–D.

claim: NRX-1L::GFP localization is not appreciably altered by acr-12 deletion.
source: NRX-1L::GFP localization is also not appreciably altered by acr-12 deletion, suggesting that the positioning of NRX-1 at presynaptic terminals occurs independently of post-synaptic receptor clustering (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: The positioning of NRX-1 at presynaptic terminals occurs independently of post-synaptic receptor clustering.
source: NRX-1L::GFP localization is also not appreciably altered by acr-12 deletion, suggesting that the positioning of NRX-1 at presynaptic terminals occurs independently of post-synaptic receptor clustering (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of effect of acr-12 deletion on NRX-1 localization.

claim: NRX-1 positioning at presynaptic sites occurs independently of post-synaptic receptor localization.
source: Our results indicate NRX-1 positioning at presynaptic sites occurs independently of post-synaptic receptor localization, and raise the intriguing possibility that NRX-1 localization to the presynaptic domain may serve as an initiation signal for developmental maturation of post-synaptic specializations in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization data in various mutant backgrounds.

claim: NRX-1 localization to the presynaptic domain may serve as an initiation signal for developmental maturation of post-synaptic specializations in GABAergic neurons.
source: Our results indicate NRX-1 positioning at presynaptic sites occurs independently of post-synaptic receptor localization, and raise the intriguing possibility that NRX-1 localization to the presynaptic domain may serve as an initiation signal for developmental maturation of post-synaptic specializations in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Mutation of the COE-type transcription factor unc-3 disrupts ACR-12 clustering in VD GABAergic neurons.
source: We have previously demonstrated that mutation of the COE-type (Collier/Olf/Ebf) transcription factor unc-3 disrupts ACR-12 clustering in VD GABAergic neurons (Barbagallo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Activity of UNC-3 is essential for the specification of cholinergic neurotransmitter identity.
source: Prior work has shown that activity of UNC-3 is essential for the specification of cholinergic neurotransmitter identity (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Mutations in the unc-17 cholinergic vesicular ACh transporter produce no appreciable changes in spine-like protrusion number or ACR-12 clusters.
source: We found that mutations in the unc-17 cholinergic vesicular ACh transporter produces no appreciable changes in spine-like protrusion number or ACR-12 clusters (Figure 6B), arguing against a strong requirement for cholinergic transmission in the formation of these structures.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 6B.

claim: Cholinergic transmission is not strongly required for the formation of spine-like protrusions and ACR-12 clusters.
source: We found that mutations in the unc-17 cholinergic vesicular ACh transporter produces no appreciable changes in spine-like protrusion number or ACR-12 clusters (Figure 6B), arguing against a strong requirement for cholinergic transmission in the formation of these structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of effect of unc-17 mutation.

claim: Mutation of unc-3 significantly reduces nrx-1L::GFP fluorescence in motor neuron cell bodies of the ventral nerve cord.
source: We found that mutation of unc-3 significantly reduces nrx-1L::GFP fluorescence in motor neuron cell bodies of the ventral nerve cord, as well as the majority of fluorescence in ventral cord processes (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 6D.

claim: Fluorescent signals indicating nrx-1 mRNA are clearly associated with cholinergic motor neuron cell bodies in wild type animals.
source: Fluorescent signals indicating nrx-1 mRNA are clearly associated with cholinergic motor neuron cell bodies (co-labeled with unc-17::GFP) in wild type animals (Figure 6E), consistent with our prior analysis using the nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter.
evidence: Supported by FISH imaging in Figure 6E.

claim: The smFISH signals for nrx-1 mRNA are strongly diminished in nrx-1(nu485) deletion mutants.
source: The smFISH signals are strongly diminished in nrx-1(nu485) deletion mutants (Figure 6E,F), confirming they accurately report nrx-1 mRNA abundance.
evidence: Supported by FISH imaging and quantification in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Labeled nrx-1 mRNA signals in cholinergic motor neurons are strikingly reduced by mutation of unc-3.
source: Labeled nrx-1 mRNA signals in cholinergic motor neurons are strikingly reduced by mutation of unc-3, consistent with the possibility that nrx-1 is a transcriptional target of unc-3 (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Supported by FISH imaging and quantification in Figure 6E,F.

claim: nrx-1 is a transcriptional target of unc-3.
source: Labeled nrx-1 mRNA signals in cholinergic motor neurons are strikingly reduced by mutation of unc-3, consistent with the possibility that nrx-1 is a transcriptional target of unc-3 (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FISH data and promoter analysis.

claim: A second nrx-1L transcriptional reporter incorporating only ~2 kb of nrx-1 regulatory sequence did not produce strong fluorescence in ventral cord motor neurons.
source: We noted that a second nrx-1L transcriptional reporter incorporating only ~2 kb of nrx-1 regulatory sequence did not produce strong fluorescence in ventral cord motor neurons (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 6D.

claim: A potential COE motif (TCCCAAAGGG) is located approximately 20 bp from the 5' end of the 4.8 kb nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter.
source: We identified a potential COE motif (TCCCAAAGGG) located approximately 20 bp from the 5' end of the 4.8 kb nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter.
evidence: This is a result of sequence analysis.

claim: Mutation of the COE motif within the 4.8 kb nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter eliminates all fluorescence from ventral cord motor neurons.
source: Mutation of this site (TCCCAAAGGG >>TAAAAAAGGG) within the 4.8 kb nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter eliminates all fluorescence from ventral cord motor neurons, while fluorescence in the processes extending from head neurons remains visible (Figure 6C,D), offering evidence that UNC-3 directly regulates nrx-1 transcription in ventral cord neurons.
evidence: Supported by imaging of the mutated reporter in Figure 6D.

claim: UNC-3 directly regulates nrx-1 transcription in ventral cord neurons.
source: Mutation of this site (TCCCAAAGGG >>TAAAAAAGGG) within the 4.8 kb nrx-1L::GFP transcriptional reporter eliminates all fluorescence from ventral cord motor neurons, while fluorescence in the processes extending from head neurons remains visible (Figure 6C,D), offering evidence that UNC-3 directly regulates nrx-1 transcription in ventral cord neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the COE motif mutation data.

claim: Cholinergic-specific expression of the nrx-1L isoform significantly restored receptor clusters in the dendritic region of unc-3 mutant animals.
source: We found that cholinergic-specific expression of the nrx-1L isoform significantly restored receptor clusters in the dendritic region of unc-3 animals (Figure 6G), indicating that the lack of ACR-12 receptor clusters in unc-3 mutants is largely driven by the absence of nrx-1 expression, although additional phenotypes associated with mutation of unc-3 may contribute (e.g. variable nerve cord defasciculation) (Barbagallo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The lack of ACR-12 receptor clusters in unc-3 mutants is largely driven by the absence of nrx-1 expression.
source: We found that cholinergic-specific expression of the nrx-1L isoform significantly restored receptor clusters in the dendritic region of unc-3 animals (Figure 6G), indicating that the lack of ACR-12 receptor clusters in unc-3 mutants is largely driven by the absence of nrx-1 expression, although additional phenotypes associated with mutation of unc-3 may contribute (e.g. variable nerve cord defasciculation) (Barbagallo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: In wild type, ACR-12 receptor clusters at the tips of spiny protrusions are submerged within the presynaptic domains of cholinergic axons, where synaptic contacts are presumably located.
source: In the wild type, ACR-12 receptor clusters at the tips of spiny protrusions are submerged within the presynaptic domains of cholinergic axons, where synaptic contacts are presumably located (Figure 7A, left).
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 7A.

claim: In nrx-1 mutants, there is a gap between the neurites of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons.
source: In nrx-1 mutants, however, we noted a gap between the neurites of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons (Figure 7A, right), suggesting that nrx-1 coordinates the extension of receptor-bearing spiny protrusions to presynaptic domains of cholinergic axons.
evidence: Supported by imaging in Figure 7A.

claim: nrx-1 coordinates the extension of receptor-bearing spiny protrusions to presynaptic domains of cholinergic axons.
source: In nrx-1 mutants, however, we noted a gap between the neurites of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons (Figure 7A, right), suggesting that nrx-1 coordinates the extension of receptor-bearing spiny protrusions to presynaptic domains of cholinergic axons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data showing the gap between pre- and postsynaptic regions.

claim: nrx-1 deletion impairs cholinergic synaptic activation of GABAergic neurons, while cholinergic transmission onto muscles remains unaffected.
source: These results, in combination with the receptor clustering defects in VD GABAergic neurons and the lack of an appreciable effect on muscle synapses described above, predict that nrx-1 deletion would impair cholinergic synaptic activation of GABAergic neurons, while cholinergic transmission onto muscles would remain unaffected.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural and molecular data, which is then tested with calcium imaging.

claim: nrx-1 deletion disrupts GABA neuron Ca2+ transients in response to cholinergic stimulation.
source: Strikingly, we found that nrx-1 deletion disrupts GABA neuron Ca2+ transients in response to cholinergic stimulation, but produces no appreciable effect on muscle Ca2+ transients, consistent with a specific requirement for nrx-1 in the development of functional connectivity between cholinergic and GABAergic neuron, but not muscle, synaptic partners (Figure 7B–G).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7B–G.

claim: nrx-1 deletion produces no appreciable effect on muscle Ca2+ transients in response to cholinergic stimulation.
source: Strikingly, we found that nrx-1 deletion disrupts GABA neuron Ca2+ transients in response to cholinergic stimulation, but produces no appreciable effect on muscle Ca2+ transients, consistent with a specific requirement for nrx-1 in the development of functional connectivity between cholinergic and GABAergic neuron, but not muscle, synaptic partners (Figure 7B–G).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7B–G.

claim: Cholinergic depolarization (5 s) evokes robust stimulus-coupled Ca2+ transients in both GABAergic neurons (67% of stimuli) and muscles (88% of stimuli) that occur within 250 ms of stimulus onset.
source: Cholinergic depolarization (5 s) evokes robust stimulus-coupled Ca2+ transients in both GABAergic neurons (67% of stimuli) and muscles (88% of stimuli) that occur within 250 ms of stimulus onset (average response latency: 0.22 ± 0.06 s in motor neurons and 0.25 ± 0.02 s in muscles).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the calcium imaging results.

claim: Evoked Ca2+ transients are not observed in the absence of cholinergic Chrimson expression or in the absence of retinal.
source: These transients are not observed in the absence of cholinergic Chrimson expression or in the absence of retinal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with a requirement for presynaptic Chrimson-mediated depolarization.
evidence: Supported by control experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Motor neuron Ca2+ transients are typically shorter in duration (mean duration: 7.7 ± 1 s in GABA neurons; 10.8 ± 0.5 s in muscles) and decay more rapidly (τdecay: 1.1 ± 0.4 s in GABA neurons; 4.6 ± 0.6 s in muscles) compared with muscle transients.
source: Motor neuron transients are typically shorter in duration (mean duration: 7.7 ± 1 s in GABA neurons; 10.8 ± 0.5 s in muscles) and decay more rapidly (τdecay: 1.1 ± 0.4 s in GABA neurons; 4.6 ± 0.6 s in muscles) compared with muscle transients, likely reflecting differences in both synaptic connectivity and physiology across the two cell types.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the calcium imaging results.

claim: acr-12 deletion reduces the mean peak amplitude of GABA neuron calcium responses to cholinergic stimulation by 60%.
source: Specifically, acr-12 deletion reduces the mean peak amplitude of GABA neuron calcium responses to cholinergic stimulation by 60% (Figure 7C–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) and increases the failure rate (no response to stimulation) by 53% compared to wild type, consistent with prior electrophysiology studies (Petrash et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7C–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, and citation to prior work.

claim: The mean peak amplitude of calcium responses to cholinergic stimulation is reduced by 95% in unc-29;acr-16 double mutants in muscles.
source: Similarly, for muscles, the mean peak amplitude of calcium responses to cholinergic stimulation is reduced by 95% in unc-29;acr-16 double mutants (Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), and the failure rate is increased roughly 15-fold to 77%, consistent with prior electrophysiology studies of evoked synaptic responses in these double mutants (Francis et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7F–G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, and citation to prior work.

claim: nrx-1 deletion reduces the mean peak amplitude of GABA neuron calcium responses to cholinergic stimulation by roughly 71%.
source: nrx-1 deletion reduces the mean peak amplitude of GABA neuron calcium responses to cholinergic stimulation by roughly 71% (Figure 7C–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), and increases the failure rate for GABA neuron recordings by 47%.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7C–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: nrx-1 deletion does not produce a significant decrease in either mean peak fluorescence or the failure rate in recordings of evoked muscle activity.
source: By comparison, nrx-1 deletion does not produce a significant decrease in either mean peak fluorescence (Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) or the failure rate in recordings of evoked muscle activity.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7F–G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both the failure rate and mean peak amplitude of evoked GABA neuron Ca2+ responses are restored to wild type levels with expression of a rescuing nrx-1L transgene in nrx-1 mutants using a cholinergic neuron-specific promoter.
source: Notably, both the failure rate and mean peak amplitude of evoked GABA neuron Ca2+ responses are restored to wild type levels with expression of a rescuing nrx-1L transgene in nrx-1 mutants using a cholinergic neuron-specific promoter (Figure 7C–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 7C–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: nrx-1 mutants display defects in the amplitude of dorsoventral bending.
source: Consistent with a requirement for NRX-1 in cholinergic synaptic connectivity with GABAergic motor neurons, automated worm track analysis showed that nrx-1 mutants display defects in the amplitude of dorsoventral bending, a feature of worm movement previously associated with GABAergic function (McIntire et al., 1993; Petrash et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by automated worm tracking data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and citations to prior work.

claim: Defects in dorsoventral bending in nrx-1 mutants are rescued with cell-specific expression of nrx-1L in cholinergic neurons.
source: These effects are rescued with cell-specific expression of nrx-1L in cholinergic neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by automated worm tracking data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Presynaptic nrx-1 expression in cholinergic neurons is required for synaptic connectivity between cholinergic and GABAergic motor neurons.
source: Thus, presynaptic nrx-1 expression in cholinergic neurons is required for synaptic connectivity between cholinergic and GABAergic motor neurons, and deficits in these connections alter motor performance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the calcium imaging and behavioral data.

claim: Deficits in cholinergic-GABAergic connections alter motor performance.
source: Thus, presynaptic nrx-1 expression in cholinergic neurons is required for synaptic connectivity between cholinergic and GABAergic motor neurons, and deficits in these connections alter motor performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral analysis.

claim: NRX-1 located in presynaptic cholinergic neurons is required for establishing synaptic connectivity with partnering GABAergic neurons, but not muscle cells.
source: Together, our data indicate that NRX-1 located in presynaptic cholinergic neurons is required for establishing synaptic connectivity with partnering GABAergic neurons, but not muscle cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings.

claim: NRX-1 signaling promotes both receptor clustering and the outgrowth of post-synaptic spine-like morphological features in GABAergic dendrites.
source: NRX-1 signaling promotes both receptor clustering and the outgrowth of post-synaptic spine-like morphological features in GABAergic dendrites.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings.

claim: Distinct synaptic organizers, acting on specific post-synaptic targets, are coordinately regulated with neuronal identity.
source: Our work suggests synaptic target-specific utilization of organizers such as neurexin may specify divergent connectivity, and provide a molecular mechanism for target-specific regulation of synapse development.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion and model based on the findings.

claim: Mutation of Drosophila neurexin (dnrx) causes disorganization of synaptic structure at the neuromuscular junction.
source: Similarly, in Drosophila, mutation of the single neurexin gene dnrx causes disorganization of synaptic structure at the neuromuscular junction (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Knockout of two out of the three mouse alpha neurexins reduces dendrite length and total spine number in the cortex.
source: Knockout of two out of the three mouse alpha neurexins reduces dendrite length and total spine number in the cortex (Dudanova et al., 2007), though significant numbers of dendritic spines remain detectable.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Dendritic spines on mouse CA1 pyramidal neurons form normally in the absence of functional glutamate receptors.
source: Similarly, dendritic spines on mouse CA1 pyramidal neurons form normally in the absence of functional glutamate receptors (Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Genes required for proper localization of muscle L-AChRs (e.g. madd-4, lev-10) play comparatively minor roles at synapses onto GABA neurons.
source: Although GABA neuron ACR-12 AChRs and muscle L-AChRs share very similar subunit composition (Boulin et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 1980), we find that genes required for proper localization of muscle L-AChRs (e.g. madd-4, lev-10) play comparatively minor roles at synapses onto GABA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the candidate gene screen data and citations to prior work.

claim: A retrograde neurexin-neuroligin signaling pathway that regulates neurotransmitter release has been described, involving signaling through the Ca2+ channel auxiliary subunit UNC-36/α2δ.
source: A retrograde neurexin-neuroligin signaling pathway that regulates neurotransmitter release has been described, involving signaling through the Ca2+ channel auxiliary subunit UNC-36/α2δ (Hu et al., 2012; Tong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Mutation of unc-36 has no appreciable effect on post-synaptic development in GABAergic neurons.
source: Consistent with this representing a distinct mechanism from that described in our work, mutation of unc-36 has no appreciable effect on post-synaptic development in our experiments.
evidence: This is a result from the candidate gene screen.

claim: Postsynaptic expression of NLG-1/neuroligin is required at GABAergic synapses.
source: Postsynaptic expression of NLG-1/neuroligin is required at GABAergic synapses. However, MADD-4/Punctin likely acts as a major presynaptic partner for NLG-1 in this case, with NRX-1 playing a comparatively minor role (Maro et al., 2015; Tong et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: MADD-4/Punctin likely acts as a major presynaptic partner for NLG-1 at GABAergic synapses, with NRX-1 playing a comparatively minor role.
source: Postsynaptic expression of NLG-1/neuroligin is required at GABAergic synapses. However, MADD-4/Punctin likely acts as a major presynaptic partner for NLG-1 in this case, with NRX-1 playing a comparatively minor role (Maro et al., 2015; Tong et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Recent work implicates neurexin-neuroligin signaling in sexually dimorphic neurite plasticity.
source: Finally, recent work also implicates neurexin-neuroligin signaling in sexually dimorphic neurite plasticity (Hart and Hobert, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Prior studies offer strong evidence for alternate neurexin binding partners that support trans-synaptic signaling.
source: Prior studies offer strong evidence for alternate neurexin binding partners that support trans-synaptic signaling (Boucard et al., 2012; de Wit et al., 2009; Ko et al., 2009; Missler et al., 1998; Petrenko et al., 1996; Pettem et al., 2013; Sugita et al., 2001; Uemura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: UNC-3 transcriptional regulation of MADD-4/Punctin is essential for proper development of cholinergic synapses with muscles.
source: Prior work indicates that UNC-3 transcriptional regulation of MADD-4/Punctin is essential for proper development of cholinergic synapses with muscles (Kratsios et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: madd-4 is dispensable for cholinergic receptor clustering in GABAergic neurons.
source: However, madd-4 is dispensable for cholinergic receptor clustering in neighboring GABAergic neurons (Barbagallo et al., 2017) (this study).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and data from this study.

claim: Cholinergic connectivity with distinct synaptic targets–muscles and GABAergic neurons–is coordinately regulated with cholinergic neuronal identity by unc-3 transcriptional control of alternate synaptic organizers.
source: Thus, cholinergic connectivity with distinct synaptic targets–muscles and GABAergic neurons–is coordinately regulated with cholinergic neuronal identity by unc-3 transcriptional control of alternate synaptic organizers.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings about unc-3 regulation of nrx-1 and madd-4.
